sections.normalized_html:

Therefore, the point of intersection in polar coordinates is [MATH: \left(2.7, \pi\right).]

sections.normalized_html:
A circle of radius [MATH: k] centered at the origin has the polar equation [MATH: r = k.]

We can compute the radius [MATH: k] of our circle using the Pythagorean theorem, as follows:

[MATH: k|= sqrt(x^{2} + y^{2}); = sqrt(2^{2} + 5^{2}); = sqrt(29)]

Therefore, the equation of the circle is [MATH: r=\sqrt{29}.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Expressing certain curves in polar coordinates turns out to be very handy in various situations due to their simplicity compared to Cartesian coordinates.

Content:
For instance, the equation of a circle of radius [MATH: 2] in polar coordinates is simply

Content:
[MATH: r = 2.]

Content:
This is significantly simpler compared to its Cartesian counterpart [MATH: x^2+y^2 = 4.]

Content:
More generally, consider a circle of radius [MATH: k] centered at the origin, as shown below.

Graphic:

Content:

Content:
You might wonder why the polar angle [MATH: \theta] does not appear in the equation. The reason is that the radius of the circle is independent of the polar angle (i.e., it is always the same, regardless of the value of [MATH: \theta]). For that reason, the polar angle does not feature in the equation.
